offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: The evidence points to Postgres pool exhaustion in payments-api that began soon after its 21:36:53 deploy. The likeliest cause is the REFUND_CONNECTION=kept setting, so I can diagnose now.

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api was redeployed at 21:36:53 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. The likely effect is that each refund request keeps its Postgres connection instead of returning it to the pool. Refunds stay fast (about 15 ms) while the pool fills. About a minute after the deploy, around 21:38, the pool ran out. From then on, every request that needs a database connection, POST /payments and refunds alike, waits for the pool timeout (about 5 s) and fails with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout, which surfaces as a 500. That produces both the 5xx ratio and the roughly 7 s p95 in the alert. The provider and Redis are healthy and fast. Still open: I could not see the previous REFUND_CONNECTION value or a pool-usage metric. The 'kept' setting as the specific leak is therefore inferred from the setting's name and the timing, not observed directly. Another change in the same deploy could be the cause, but a rollback of that deploy would cover it as well.

evidence.shows: POST /payments 500s start only at 21:38:04 (1.3/s), reach 5.35/s at 21:38:34, and 201s drop to 0.46/s. This confirms the alert.
payments-api is the only service deployed after the 21:35:26 stack start, at 21:36:53, about 1 minute before the 500s began. Its settings include REFUND_CONNECTION=kept.
All payments-api errors are psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout on POST /payments, meaning the Postgres connection pool is exhausted.
Slow POST /payments traces since 21:38:04 take 5.9–6.9 s.
A slow trace has no provider or DB spans. A Redis SET at 1.7 s is followed by about 5 s of nothing, then a Redis EVAL and a 500 with PoolTimeout. The request spent that time waiting on the pool.
Provider call p95 stays about 5 ms throughout, so the provider is not slow and is not holding connections.

Before 21:38, refund and payment routes took 14–38 ms on average. Both jumped to 4–6 s at 21:38:14, consistent with a shared pool being exhausted. Refunds were not slow beforehand, which fits connections being leaked rather than held during long work.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to its settings before the 21:36:53 deploy, presumably a REFUND_CONNECTION mode that returns connections to the pool. Recreating the container also frees the leaked connections. Then confirm that the POST /payments 5xx rate and latency return to baseline. Run money_check to verify that refunds and payments made during the incident match the provider.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, so in-flight payment and refund requests may fail. Clients should retry with idempotency keys stored in Redis. If the cause is something other than this deploy, the rollback will not stop the exhaustion. Payments that failed with 500 may need to be retried by clients. Nothing already booked is repaired.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the rollback makes things worse, redeploy the current payments-api settings (image sha256:6352144993c2 with PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept). Then investigate pool sizing and connection handling directly.
